name: etcd
summary: A distributed, strongly consistent key-value store that uses Raft-backed revisions, transactional comparisons, watches, and leases for coordination and configuration state.

features.name: Raft-backed linearizable key-value API
features.description: etcd exposes a key-value API whose linearizable operations are coordinated through a Raft-replicated state machine. The API separates linearizable reads from serializable reads and documents the corresponding guarantees.
benefits: Provides a clear consistency contract for coordination state
costs: Quorum loss prevents progress for operations requiring linearizability
Consensus and persistence add latency compared with a local map
Read mode selection is an application correctness decision

features.name: MVCC revisioned key history
features.description: The v3 key-value model assigns revisions to committed changes and retains historical versions subject to compaction. Reads can address a revision, while deletes create tombstones in the revisioned history.
benefits: Gives clients a monotonic point of observation
Supports historical reads and consistent watch positions
Makes compaction an explicit history-lifetime policy
costs: Uncompacted history consumes storage and memory
Compaction invalidates requests for older revisions
Revision semantics do not make external side effects transactional

features.name: Transactional compare-and-swap
features.description: The etcd transaction API evaluates comparisons against key metadata or values and atomically applies one branch of operations. This supports conditional updates and multi-key coordination within one etcd transaction.
benefits: Combines preconditions and mutations in one state-machine operation
Supports locks, elections, and guarded configuration changes
Makes conflict conditions explicit in the request
costs: Transactions are bounded by the etcd API and do not cover external resources
Large or contended transactions increase consensus and storage work
Clients must handle aborted comparisons and retries

features.name: Watch streams and leases
features.description: Clients can watch changes from a revision and attach keys to leases whose expiration removes associated keys. Watch streams and lease keep-alives expose state changes and liveness through the API.
benefits: Enables event-driven consumers instead of polling
Ties ephemeral coordination state to renewable liveness
Allows consumers to resume from a known revision when history remains
costs: Slow watchers can encounter compaction or backpressure conditions
Lease expiry depends on server timing and keep-alive behavior
Consumers must reconcile state after stream interruption

mathematical_views.question: How do committed mutations induce a single revisioned key-value history across members?
assumptions: Raft commitment is modeled as the source of the authoritative mutation order
Each committed operation advances a logical revision observable by the API
The model abstracts election timing, transport failures, and backend layout
Linearizability claims apply only to operations using the documented linearizable path

mathematical_views.model: Revision-indexed lease and watch transition system
mathematical_views.question: When can a consumer reconstruct current coordination state from watched revisions and lease events?
assumptions: A watcher begins from a valid revision that has not been compacted
Events are processed in revision order and the consumer can re-read after interruption
Lease expiry is modeled as a server-side deletion transition
The view does not infer exactly-once external effects

benefits: Strong coordination semantics backed by replicated state
costs: Quorum and consensus latency constrain availability and throughput

benefits: Consistent observations and resumable change positions
costs: History retention and compaction create storage and recovery trade-offs

benefits: Atomic guarded mutations across multiple keys
costs: Scope stops at etcd and conflicts require client retry logic

benefits: Efficient change propagation and liveness-bound records
costs: Stream recovery, compaction, and expiry require reconciliation
